clues.clue: Diagnosed with ALS at age 21, this physicist went on to write the bestseller 'A Brief History of Time'.
A mold spore that drifted into this Scot's untidy London lab in 1928 pointed the way to penicillin.
This Russian chemist left gaps in his 1869 table for elements like gallium, later found just as he predicted.
This Danish astronomer lost part of his nose in a 1566 duel and wore a metal replacement.
A 1913 letter packed with theorems to G.H. Hardy carried this self-taught Indian mathematician to Cambridge.
This automaker's moving assembly line sent the price of his Model T plummeting after 1913.
In 1793 this Yale grad invented the cotton gin, transforming the economy of the American South.
This portrait painter turned inventor telegraphed 'What hath God wrought' from Washington in 1844.
This Black inventor from Cleveland patented a lifesaving safety hood and a three-position traffic signal.
Burrs stuck to this Swiss engineer's dog on a hunt, inspiring the hook-and-loop fastener he named Velcro.
This leader's 1930 Salt March defied a British monopoly on an everyday seasoning.
Fined $100 for voting in the 1872 presidential election, this suffragist never paid a cent.
With Dolores Huerta, this labor leader co-founded the farmworkers' union behind a national grape boycott.
Chicago's Hull House made this social reformer the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Parliament ended the British slave trade in 1807 after this evangelical MP's 20-year crusade.
Legend ties this Spanish explorer of Florida to a search for the Fountain of Youth.
This Norse sailor reached a land he called Vinland around 1000 A.D., centuries before Columbus.
Aboard the Golden Hind, this Elizabethan sea dog completed a circumnavigation of the globe in 1580.
This Ming dynasty admiral led seven treasure-fleet voyages, sailing as far as East Africa.
This Prussian naturalist's five-year American trek left his name on a current, a penguin and many peaks.
In 1932 this aviator became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
This French ocean explorer co-invented the Aqua-Lung and sailed the research ship Calypso.
This Sherpa mountaineer stood atop Everest with Edmund Hillary on May 29, 1953.
In 1947 this Norwegian sailed the balsa raft Kon-Tiki some 4,300 miles from Peru to Polynesia.
With Don Walsh, this Swiss oceanographer took the bathyscaphe Trieste to the Mariana Trench floor in 1960.
This British monarch's white gown at her 1840 wedding to Prince Albert set a bridal trend for the ages.
Traveling incognito in 1697, this Russian tsar swung a hammer in Dutch shipyards to master shipbuilding.
Between campaigns on the Danube, this Roman emperor jotted the Stoic notes we call 'Meditations'.
This 15th century Korean king oversaw the creation of Hangul, an alphabet in daily use ever since.
This Swedish queen shocked Europe by abdicating in 1654, converting to Catholicism and settling in Rome.
This sitting vice president fatally wounded Alexander Hamilton in an 1804 duel at Weehawken.
This Celtics legend's rivalry with Magic Johnson began in the 1979 NCAA championship game.
The play and film 'Amadeus' cast this Italian court composer as Mozart's jealous rival.
Isaac Newton feuded bitterly with this German polymath over who invented calculus first.
Edward Drinker Cope's fossil feud with this Yale paleontologist came to be called the Bone Wars.
This actor shared a screenwriting Oscar with childhood pal Matt Damon for 1997's 'Good Will Hunting'.
This 'Lord of the Rings' author swapped drafts with C.S. Lewis in an Oxford circle called the Inklings.
Vincent van Gogh shared the Yellow House at Arles with this painter until their friendship imploded.
Henry David Thoreau built his Walden Pond cabin on land owned by this essayist, his friend and mentor.
Franz Kafka told this loyal friend to burn his manuscripts; instead he published 'The Trial'.
This Shoshone teenager crossed the West with Lewis and Clark, interpreting with her baby son in tow.
This NASA mathematician of 'Hidden Figures' fame double-checked the orbital math for John Glenn's 1962 flight.
This reporter feigned insanity to expose an asylum, then circled the globe in 72 days for the New York World.
This British chemist's X-ray image of DNA, the famed Photo 51, guided Watson and Crick to the double helix.
Element 109 honors this physicist, who explained nuclear fission with her nephew yet never won a Nobel.
This British singer titled her albums '19', '21', '25' and '30' after milestones of her own age.
Born François-Marie Arouet, this French wit skewered rosy optimism in 'Candide'.
This Dutch master of 'The Night Watch' also painted dozens of self-portraits over four decades.
This 16th century French seer published the cryptic quatrains of 'Les Prophéties' in 1555.
A mob killed this woman philosopher and mathematician of ancient Alexandria in 415 A.D.
A Milan convent wall bears 'The Last Supper', this Renaissance master's mural of a final meal.
This last emperor of China, subject of a 1987 Best Picture winner, later tended a Beijing botanical garden.
This Apollo 17 commander was the final astronaut of the Apollo program to walk on the Moon.
This Marylander, the last surviving signer of the Declaration of Independence, died in 1832.
Moments before a sharpshooter's bullet struck, this Union general scoffed that the enemy 'couldn't hit an elephant at this distance'.

name: AND NOW FOR MY NEXT ACT

clues.clue: This Austrian-born bodybuilding champ became 'The Terminator', then governor of California in 2003.
This preacher and grill pitchman reclaimed boxing's heavyweight crown in 1994 at age 45.
This designer spent 17 years at Vogue and two at Ralph Lauren before opening her bridal salon in 1990.
Arthritis turned this upstate New York farm wife from embroidery to folk painting in her late 70s.
This French poet gave up verse by about age 21 to trade coffee and firearms in the Horn of Africa.
